kurals.tamil:
சீரிடம் காணின் எறிதற்குப் பட்டடை
நேரா நிரந்தவர் நட்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Seeridam kaanin erithar̲kup pattadai
neraa niranthavar natpu.
kurals.meaning: The friendship of people who keep company with you without being one with you in heart is like an anvil: it seems to hold you up, but it is really the base on which you will be struck down once they find the right moment.
kurals.elementary: A blacksmith’s anvil looks like a strong, steady table, but its real job is to hold the metal still so the hammer can hit it. A fake friend can feel like solid support, but they are only holding you in place until it suits them to let you get hurt.
kurals.university: The chapter title kooḍaa naṭpu (கூடா நட்பு) means ‘friendship that does not truly join’, and this opening couplet defines it: those who are neraa (நேரா, not inwardly agreeing) yet niranthavar (நிரந்தவர், outwardly close). Paṭṭaḍai (பட்டடை) is the smith’s anvil, the block on which metal is laid to be cut; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read the simile this way, Pappaiah adding that it looks like support while really serving the cutting. Seer-idam (சீரிடம்) is ‘the fitting place or occasion’, so the danger lies in timing: the false friend waits for an opening. Parimelazhagar places this chapter after Thee Natpu (82, evil friendship) as a treatment of friendship that is enmity in disguise, a theme he reads in a royal-political frame. The couplet is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After the war, the blind king Dhritarashtra asks to embrace Bhima. Krishna, sensing his grief-driven rage, pushes forward an iron statue of Bhima instead, and the old king crushes it to pieces in what was meant to look like a loving embrace.
hinduism.explanation: An embrace, the most intimate sign of affection, is turned into the very means of destruction once the chance appears.
hinduism.tie_back: Like Valluvar’s anvil, the embrace looks like support but is the place where the blow is meant to fall.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong image of hostile intent hidden in an embrace, though Dhritarashtra acts from grief rather than long-planned false friendship; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And from that time he sought opportunity to betray him.”
christianity.explanation: Judas remains among the twelve, sharing their life, while secretly waiting for the right moment to hand Jesus over.
christianity.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s ‘when they find the fitting moment’: closeness kept up while waiting for the chance to strike.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match on companionship that waits for its opportunity; the anvil image is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: “How [can there be a treaty] while, if they gain dominance over you, they do not observe concerning you any pact of kinship or covenant of protection? They satisfy you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse [compliance], and most of them are defiantly disobedient.”
islam.explanation: The verse describes allies whose words please while their hearts refuse, and who will honour no bond once they gain the upper hand.
islam.tie_back: Pleasing outwardly, hostile inwardly, and waiting for the advantage: the same anatomy as the Kural’s false friend.
islam._accuracy_note: Close thematic match, though the Qur’anic context is a specific treaty situation rather than personal friendship.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Their tongue is a sharpened arrow, / They use their mouths to deceive. / They speak to their fellows in friendship, / But lay an ambush for them in their hearts.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah describes a society where friendly speech covers a heart that is lying in wait.
judaism.tie_back: Friendly speech outside, an ambush inside: Valluvar’s anvil waiting for its moment.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on outward friendship concealing an ambush.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “These four, young householder, should be understood as foes in the guise of friends: (1) he who appropriates a friend's possessions, (2) he who renders lip-service, (3) he who flatters, (4) he who brings ruin.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches the layman Sigala to recognise four kinds of people who look like friends but act as enemies.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Foes in the guise of friends’ is almost a definition of the Kural’s kooḍaa naṭpu.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same category of false friend; the Kural’s specific emphasis on waiting for an opportunity is not in this passage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He asked me to his house, feasted me, and then butchered me most miserably as though I were a fat beast in a slaughter house”
greek_mythology.explanation: Agamemnon’s ghost tells Odysseus how Aegisthus welcomed him home with a feast, the very act of hospitality becoming the trap.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The feast is the anvil: a show of welcome that is really the place prepared for the blow.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on hospitality masking a planned killing; Aegisthus was an open rival rather than a long-standing friend.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “when he has been deceived by the pretences of the other person, it is just that he should complain against his deceiver; he will complain with more justice than one does against people who counterfeit the currency, inasmuch as the wrongdoing is concerned with something more valuable.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle treats pretended friendship as worse than forging money, because what is counterfeited is more precious.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers see feigned friendship as a counterfeit that does its harm precisely because it is trusted.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.3 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the moral judgment of feigned friendship, but lacks the Kural’s image of a friend waiting to strike.

kurals.tamil:
இனம்போன்று இனமல்லார் கேண்மை மகளிர்
மனம்போல வேறு படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Inampondru inamallaar kenmai magalir
manampola veru padum.
kurals.meaning: The friendship of those who act like your own people but are not, will shift and change according to what they can gain, never holding one steady form.
kurals.elementary: Some kids are your friend only when you have the best snack at lunch. The day you have nothing to share, they sit somewhere else. Their friendship changes shape depending on what they can get.
kurals.university: Inam (இனம்) means one’s own circle or kin; inam-pondru inam-allaar are those who resemble kin but are not. Kenmai (கேண்மை) is intimacy or friendship. The comparison with magalir manam (மகளிர் மனம்) is read by Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar, Puliyur Kesigan) specifically as the mind of courtesans (பொதுமகளிர் / விலைமகளிர்), whose affection follows payment, not as a judgment on women in general; Puliyur Kesigan glosses the point as changing ‘according to the gain received’. The comparison reflects the social assumptions of its age, but its logical point is clear: an attachment driven by gain changes when the gain changes. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha’s first book, a jackal makes friends with a deer by flattering it, while really hoping to feed on it; the deer ignores the warnings of its old friend the crow until it is caught in a snare, and the jackal waits for it to die.
hinduism.explanation: The fable shows a newcomer who copies the language of friendship but is moved only by what he can gain.
hinduism.tie_back: The jackal is ‘like kin but not kin’, and his friendship turns as soon as profit points elsewhere.
hinduism.source: Hitopadesha, Book I (Mitralabha), the deer, the crow and the jackal
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good thematic match told from memory of a well-known fable; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
christianity.explanation: James warns that a divided heart produces a life with no fixed direction.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s false friend is ‘double-minded’ in just this sense, so his friendship keeps shifting.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of instability from a divided heart, but James speaks of faith and prayer, not friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with their evil ones, they say, "Indeed, we are with you; we were only mockers."”
islam.explanation: The hypocrites present themselves as one with the believers but change their words as soon as the company changes.
islam.tie_back: They ‘seem like our own people but are not’, and their loyalty shifts with the room, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on seeming kinship that changes with the audience.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Each of you, beware of your friend! / Trust not even your kinsfolk! / For every sibling takes advantage, / Every friend deals basely.”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah laments a time when even those who look like family and friends seek their own advantage.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts warn that the look of kinship guarantees nothing when advantage rules the heart.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on kin-like people who cannot be trusted; Jeremiah’s is a prophetic lament, not practical counsel.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One is a bottle friend; one says, 'friend, friend' only to one's face; one is a friend and an associate only when it is advantageous.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists kinds of companions whose friendship lasts only as long as it is convenient or profitable.
buddhism.tie_back: A friend ‘only when it is advantageous’ is the Kural’s gain-driven friendship that changes form.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close on friendship that depends on advantage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Aesop’s fable of the bat and the weasels, a bat caught by one weasel claims to be a mouse, and caught by another that hates mice claims to be a bird, changing what it is to suit whoever holds it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bat survives by switching sides, belonging fully to no one.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s false kin likewise change their colours according to what each moment offers.
greek_mythology.source: Aesop’s Fables, ‘The Bat and the Weasels’ (Townsend translation)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures the changeable loyalty, but it is a fable of self-preservation rather than a story about false friendship; Aesop is Greek fable, not myth proper.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For the essence of friendship being that two minds become as one, how can that ever take place if the mind of each of the separate parties to it is not single and uniform, but variable, changeable, and complex?”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero argues that friendship requires a steady, single-minded character, and that a changeable mind makes it impossible.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s point is the same: a heart that ‘changes’ cannot hold a real friendship.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near match on changeability as the mark of false friendship.

kurals.tamil:
பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து மனநல்லர்
ஆகுதல் மாணார்க் கரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Palanalla kat̲rak kadaiththu mananallar
aaguthal maanaark karithu.
kurals.meaning: Even after they have studied many good books, it is hard for people who lack inner nobility to become truly good-hearted toward you.
kurals.elementary: You can read every book about kindness and still be unkind. Knowing the rules of a game does not make you a fair player. A person who doesn’t care about you can learn lots of nice words without their heart changing.
kurals.university: Pala nalla katrak kadaiththu (பலநல்ல கற்றக் கடைத்து) means ‘even when it happens that they have learned many good things’; mana-nallar (மனநல்லர்) are the good-hearted. Maanaar (மாணார்) literally means ‘those who are not excellent’; Varadarasanar glosses it as those who have not attained greatness through inner affection, while Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as those hostile at heart (பகையுணர்வு படைத்தோர்), and Pope’s gloss ‘enemies’ follows the latter. The couplet thus warns against assuming that a learned enemy has been softened by learning: knowledge of virtue is not virtue. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Vasishtha Dharmasutra teaches that the Vedas, even learned in full with their auxiliary sciences, do not purify a person who lacks good conduct.
hinduism.explanation: The dharma tradition holds that sacred learning is no substitute for character.
hinduism.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: much learning does not make a bad heart good.
hinduism.source: Vasishtha Dharmasutra 6.3 (trans. Georg Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 14)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Thematic match given as paraphrase; exact wording not verified against a live text this session.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul insists that knowledge without love has no worth.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts separate knowing much from being good at heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on knowledge without love; Paul is not speaking of enemies or false friends specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares those who carry scripture without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: Learning carried but not taken to heart is the Kural’s learned man who stays unkind.
islam._accuracy_note: Clear match on learning that does not change the heart; the verse targets a specific community, not false friends.

judaism.quote_or_event: “one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah teaches that wisdom without matching deeds has no roots.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s learned but ill-hearted person is a tree of many branches with no root of goodness.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (trans. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on learning outrunning character; does not address enmity.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that reciting scripture without practising it leaves a person outside its benefits.
buddhism.tie_back: Same insight: many good texts studied do not make a good heart.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on learning without practice; not focused on enemies.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Daedalus, the most gifted craftsman of Athens, grew jealous of his nephew and pupil Perdix (also called Talos), who had invented the saw, and threw him from the Acropolis.
greek_mythology.explanation: Supreme skill and knowledge did not prevent envy from ruling Daedalus’s heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s learned enemy, great learning left the heart unchanged.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates skill without goodness, but is not about friendship; summarised.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus says that much learning does not teach understanding, otherwise it would have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, Xenophanes and Hecataeus.
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus mocks famous learned men for amassing information without insight.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise denies that wide reading produces a sound heart.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, fragment DK 22 B40 (preserved in Diogenes Laertius 9.1)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Heraclitus means intellectual insight rather than goodness of heart; paraphrased, wording not verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா
வஞ்சரை அஞ்சப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mugaththin iniya nagaaa agaththinnaa
vanjarai anjap padum.
kurals.meaning: Be wary of deceivers who smile sweetly with their faces while their hearts are bitter toward you.
kurals.elementary: A shiny red apple can still have a worm inside. A big smile on the outside does not always mean kindness on the inside, so it is wise to watch what people do, not just how they smile.
kurals.university: The couplet sets mugam (முகம், face) against agam (அகம், the inner self), a pairing that will return in Kural 830. Nagaaa (நகாஅ, ‘smiling’) shows alapeḍai, the metrical lengthening of a vowel, and akaththinnaa (அகத்து இன்னா) means ‘bitter or harmful within’. Vanjar (வஞ்சர்) are deceivers, and anjappaḍum (அஞ்சப்படும்) is the impersonal ‘is to be feared’; Varadarasanar reads it as fearing to make friends with them, Kalaignar as fearing them and keeping away. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kamsa sends the demoness Putana to kill the infant Krishna. She comes as a beautiful, affectionate woman, takes the child lovingly and offers him her breast, which she has smeared with poison; Krishna draws out her life instead.
hinduism.explanation: A face of tenderness hides a murderous purpose.
hinduism.tie_back: Putana is the Kural’s sweet face over a bitter heart, in its most vivid form.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong image of loving appearance over deadly intent; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns of people whose gentle appearance hides a predatory heart.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Beware’ of the gentle outside and the wolf inside is exactly the Kural’s ‘fear those who smile but are bitter within’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near match on outward gentleness hiding inner hostility; Jesus’s target is false teachers.

islam.quote_or_event: “And of the people is he whose speech pleases you in worldly life, and he calls Allah to witness as to what is in his heart, yet he is the fiercest of opponents.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a man whose pleasant words and pious oaths cover deep hostility.
islam.tie_back: Pleasing on the surface, the fiercest opponent beneath: the Kural’s smiling deceiver.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on pleasing exterior and hostile interior.

judaism.quote_or_event: “with talk smoother than butter, / yet with a mind set on war; / with words that were softer than oil, / yet in fact were drawn swords.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes a former companion whose soft words hid a mind bent on war.
judaism.tie_back: Smooth words outside, swords within: the same split the Kural tells us to fear.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; the psalm speaks of a betraying companion, as the chapter does.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the use of your matted hair, O witless man? What of your garment of antelope's hide? Within you is the tangle (of passion); only outwardly do you cleanse yourself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rebukes a man whose outward ascetic appearance hides inner corruption.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts warn that a pleasing outside can conceal what is tangled within.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the outer/inner contrast but concerns religious hypocrisy, not a smiling enemy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe welcomes Odysseus’s men graciously into her hall and serves them a pleasant mixture of cheese, barley, honey and wine, into which she has put drugs; then she strikes them with her wand and turns them into swine.
greek_mythology.explanation: Warm hospitality is the vehicle of the harm.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Circe’s gracious welcome over a harmful purpose is the sweet face and bitter heart of the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on welcoming manner hiding harm; summarised, not quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon argues that the height of injustice is to seem just without being just, so that the unjust man wears a reputation for goodness while doing harm.
philosophy.explanation: Plato poses the problem of the person whose appearance of virtue is a mask.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s deceiver is the person who seems good to our face but is not good to us.
philosophy.source: Plato, Republic, Book II (trans. Benjamin Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the seeming-versus-being theme in general terms; paraphrased, not verified verbatim.

kurals.tamil:
மனத்தின் அமையா தவரை எனைத்தொன்றும்
சொல்லினால் தேறற்பாற்று அன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththin amaiyaa thavarai enaiththondrum
sollinaal ther̲ar̲paat̲ru andru.
kurals.meaning: In no matter whatever should you rely on the words of people who are not one with you in heart.
kurals.elementary: If someone keeps promising to share their toys but never does, you learn to stop believing the promise. Words are easy to say. When someone does not really care about you, what they say is not something to lean on.
kurals.university: Manaththin amaiyaathavar (மனத்தின் அமையாதவர்) are ‘those not settled with us in mind’; enaiththondrum (எனைத்தொன்றும்) means ‘in anything at all’. Theraṟpaaṯru anru (தேறற்பாற்று அன்று) means ‘it is not fit to be trusted or relied upon’, using theṟal (தேறல், clear conviction), the same root as the chapter Therindhu Thelidhal (51) on testing before trusting. Varadarasanar reads it as not trusting their words in any undertaking, and Kalaignar as not being able to reach any clear decision on such people’s words. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He who trusts the words, true or false, of a foe, meets with destruction like a seeker of honey, in a pit covered with dry grass.”
hinduism.explanation: In Bhishma’s tale of the bird Pujani and King Brahmadatta, the bird refuses to trust the king’s soothing words after enmity has arisen.
hinduism.tie_back: ‘The words, true or false, of a foe’ are not to be relied on: the Kural’s exact rule.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on not relying on a foe’s words.

christianity.quote_or_event: “My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: John teaches that real love is shown in action and truth, not in speech alone.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts refuse to treat words as proof of a loving heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the word-versus-heart distinction, but it is an exhortation to love rather than a warning about false friends.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see them, their forms please you, and if they speak, you listen to their speech. [They are] as if they were pieces of wood propped up - they think that every shout is against them. They are the enemy, so beware of them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns that the hypocrites’ appearance and speech are attractive but hollow, and that they are to be guarded against.
islam.tie_back: Attractive speech from those not one with you in heart is not to be trusted, as the Kural says.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on persuasive speech from the inwardly hostile.

judaism.quote_or_event: “An enemy dissembles with his speech, / Inwardly he harbors deceit. / Though he be fair-spoken do not trust him, / For seven abominations are in his mind.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs warns that fair speech from someone hostile within must not be trusted.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Though he be fair-spoken do not trust him’ is virtually the Kural restated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who renders lip-service be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he makes friendly profession as regards the past, (ii) he makes friendly profession as regards the future, (iii) he tries to gain one's favor by empty words, (iv) when opportunity for service has arisen, he expresses his inability.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha describes the friend whose friendship lives only in words.
buddhism.tie_back: The lip-service friend’s ‘empty words’ are exactly what the Kural says not to rely on.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on words without heart.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rejects Agamemnon’s gift-laden embassy, refusing to be won over by words that do not match the heart behind them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles, like Valluvar, will not rely on the words of one whose heart is elsewhere.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on words divorced from the heart.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Friendship, in which, unless you both see and show an open breast, to use a common expression, you can neither trust nor be certain of anything--no, not even of mutual affection, since you cannot be sure of its sincerity.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero says that without openness of heart, nothing a friend says can be relied on.
philosophy.tie_back: Where the heart is not open and one with ours, the Kural likewise says words cannot be trusted.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 26 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on trust depending on an open, united heart.

kurals.tamil:
நட்டார்போல் நல்லவை சொல்லினும் ஒட்டார்சொல்
ஒல்லை உணரப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nattaarpol nallavai sollinum ottaarsol
ollai unarap padum.
kurals.meaning: Even when enemies say good things as if they were friends, the real nature of their words is soon seen through.
kurals.elementary: A wolf can try to sound like a sheep, but sooner or later it growls. When someone who doesn’t like you starts talking sweetly, listen carefully; the truth usually shows up quickly.
kurals.university: Naṭṭaar (நட்டார்) are friends, those who have made friendship, and oṭṭaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not ‘stick’ or join with us, that is, foes. Nallavai sollinum (நல்லவை சொல்லினும்) concedes that the words themselves may be good, and ollai (ஒல்லை) means ‘quickly’. The couplet is partly reassurance: false friendship tends to betray itself in speech, and Kalaignar says the meanness in such words will come out without fail. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the ‘understanding’ as recognising quickly that the words are not truly meant for our good. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When the golden deer (the demon Maricha in disguise) is shot by Rama and cries out for help in Rama’s voice, Sita is frightened, but Lakshmana at once recognises the call as a demon’s trick and insists that no one could harm Rama.
hinduism.explanation: The enemy’s imitation of a beloved voice is seen through by the alert listener.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point that hostile words dressed as friendly ones are quickly understood by the discerning.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the quick detection of a disguised enemy voice, though Sita herself was not persuaded by Lakshmana; summarised.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what people really are becomes evident from what they produce.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts trust that hidden hostility reveals itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good match on revealed character; Jesus points to deeds, the Kural to words.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if We willed, We could show them to you, and you would know them by their mark; but you will surely know them by the tone of [their] speech.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says the hypocrites will be recognised by the very way they speak.
islam.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the foe’s words, however friendly, quickly give him away.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on recognising hidden enmity through speech.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His hatred may be concealed by dissimulation, / But his evil will be exposed to public view.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that disguised hatred will come into the open.
judaism.tie_back: Same confidence as the Kural that false friendliness is soon unmasked.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; Proverbs speaks of public exposure rather than personal discernment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It's through dealing with a person that his purity may be known, and then only after a long period, not a short period; by one who is attentive, not by one who is inattentive; by one who is discerning, not by one who is not discerning.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that integrity is revealed through dealings, to an attentive and discerning observer.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say a false friend’s nature can be read; the Buddha adds that it takes time and attention.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of discerning true character, but stresses a long period where the Kural says ‘quickly’.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Homeric Hymn to Hermes, the infant Hermes steals Apollo’s cattle and then denies it with innocent, sweet-sounding speeches, but Apollo sees through the lies at once and drags him before Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Charming, innocent words do not hide the truth from a discerning listener.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As the Kural says, the real meaning behind fair words is soon understood.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Captures quick detection of deceptive words, but Hermes is a playful trickster, not a false friend; summarised.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “But if we only take reasonable care, it is as easy to separate and distinguish a genuine from a specious friend as anything else that is coloured and artificial from what is sincere and genuine.”
philosophy.explanation: Cicero holds that, with reasonable care, a false friend is as easy to detect as anything counterfeit.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero and Valluvar share the confidence that the specious friend is readily seen through.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Amicitia 25 (trans. E. S. Shuckburgh)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the detectability of false friendship.

kurals.tamil:
சொல்வணக்கம் ஒன்னார்கண் கொள்ளற்க வில்வணக்கம்
தீங்கு குறித்தமை யான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Solvanakkam onnaarkan kollar̲ka vilvanakkam
theengu kur̲iththamai yaan.
kurals.meaning: Do not take a foe’s humble, bowing speech at face value: a bow bends low only in order to do harm.
kurals.elementary: When an archer pulls back a bow, it bends down low, almost like it is bowing politely. But that bend is what sends the arrow flying. Sometimes people who don’t like you act extra polite right before they try to hurt you.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pun in vaṇakkam (வணக்கம்), which means both ‘bowing, reverence’ and ‘bending’: sol-vaṇakkam is ‘humility in speech’, vil-vaṇakkam ‘the bending of a bow’. Onnaar (ஒன்னார்) are those who are not one with us, enemies. Since the bow’s bend ‘signals harm’ (theengu kuṟiththamaiyaan, தீங்கு குறித்தமையான்), a foe’s deferential words should be read the same way; Pappaiah and Kalaignar draw out the simile in this sense, and Pope translates ‘pliant speech’ and ‘pliant bow’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Ravana, planning to abduct Sita, approaches her hermitage disguised as a gentle wandering ascetic, praising her with courteous and reverent words until she offers him hospitality; then he reveals his true form and carries her off.
hinduism.explanation: Humble, respectful speech is the opening move of an act of violence.
hinduism.tie_back: Ravana’s bowing words are the bent bow of the Kural, curved for harm.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on deferential speech masking hostile intent; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?”
christianity.explanation: Judas greets Jesus with a disciple’s kiss of respect, the agreed signal for his arrest.
christianity.tie_back: A gesture of reverence used as the trigger for harm is the Kural’s bending bow.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on respectful gesture as instrument of betrayal; a kiss rather than words.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not take as intimates those other than yourselves, for they will not spare you [any] ruin. They wish you would have hardship. Hatred has already appeared from their mouths, and what their breasts conceal is greater.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an warns against taking as intimates those whose words already betray hostility and whose hearts hide more.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it tells believers not to accept hostile people’s outward speech as friendship.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches the warning against foes’ speech, but lacks the image of humble, bowing words.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Wounds by a loved one are long lasting; / The kisses of an enemy are profuse.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts a true friend’s honest blows with an enemy’s lavish shows of affection.
judaism.tie_back: An enemy’s profuse kisses are the foe’s humble words that the Kural says not to accept.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on excessive affection from an enemy; translations of this verse vary (KJV ‘deceitful’).

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In four ways, young householder, should one who flatters be understood as a foe in the guise of a friend: (i) he approves of his friend's evil deeds, (ii) he disapproves his friend's good deeds, (iii) he praises him in his presence, (iv) he speaks ill of him in his absence.”
buddhism.explanation: The flatterer praises to your face and undermines you behind your back.
buddhism.tie_back: His praise is the respectful ‘bowing’ speech that the Kural says hides harm.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on deferential speech with hostile intent; the bow image is absent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Agamemnon returns from Troy, Clytemnestra greets him with an elaborate, flattering speech of welcome and has rich purple tapestries spread for him to walk on into the palace, where she then kills him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Extravagant reverence is the prelude to murder.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Clytemnestra’s bowing welcome is the Kural’s bent bow: deference that signals harm.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on humble, honouring words preceding harm; summarised, not quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Sun Tzu advises that when the enemy’s envoys use humble words while the enemy steps up its preparations, it is a sign that he is about to advance.
philosophy.explanation: Strategic thought reads humility from a foe as a warning, not a reassurance.
philosophy.tie_back: Sun Tzu and Valluvar both read a foe’s humble speech the way one reads a drawn bow.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War, Chapter IX (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close match in substance; paraphrased because the exact Giles wording could not be verified this session.

kurals.tamil:
தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் படையொடுங்கும் ஒன்னார்
அழுதகண் ணீரும் அனைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thozhuthagai yullum padaiyodungum onnaar
azhuthagan neerum anaiththu.
kurals.meaning: A weapon may lie hidden even in the hands that foes join in worship toward you, and the tears they shed are of the same kind.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone bowing to you with hands pressed together, but hiding a water balloon behind them. Pretend sadness can be a trick too. If someone has been mean to you, a show of respect or tears doesn’t always mean they have changed.
kurals.university: Thozhuthagai (தொழுதகை) is the hand joined in worship or salutation, and paḍai oḍungum (படை ஒடுங்கும்) means ‘a weapon lies concealed’. The second line extends the image: onnaar azhutha kaṇṇeer (ஒன்னார் அழுத கண்ணீர், the tears foes have wept) is anaiththu (அனைத்து, of that same kind). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the couplet literally as a weapon concealed in the worshipping hand, and Kalaignar adds that even in weeping their hearts are full of plotting. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; thirukkural.net prints the words as தொழுதகை யுள்ளும் and கண் ணீரும் with the same metrical division.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “And O Bharata, speak soft words before thou smitest and even while thou art smiting! After the smiting is over, pity the victim, and grieve for him, and even shed tears.”
hinduism.explanation: The minister Kanika gives Dhritarashtra a cynical lesson in statecraft: gentle words and tears can be used as cover for violence.
hinduism.tie_back: Kanika’s counsel is the exact practice the Kural warns about: a foe’s tears that are part of the weapon.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 142, Kanika’s counsel (Ganguli translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, given from the deceiver’s side; the epic presents Kanika’s counsel as crooked policy, not dharma.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And he sent them to Bethlehem, and said, Go and search diligently for the young child; and when ye have found him, bring me word again, that I may come and worship him also.”
christianity.explanation: Herod claims he wants to worship the child, while planning to kill him.
christianity.tie_back: Herod’s ‘worship’ is the worshipping hand with a weapon hidden inside.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on worship as a cover for murderous intent.

islam.quote_or_event: “Here you are loving them but they are not loving you, while you believe in the Scripture - all of it. And when they meet you, they say, "We believe." But when they are alone, they bite their fingertips at you in rage.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes people who profess faith to the believers’ faces but rage against them in private.
islam.tie_back: Their profession of belief is the joined hand, and their private rage the hidden weapon.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches outward devotion hiding hostility; there is no image of tears or weapons.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Joab said to Amasa, “How are you, brother?” and with his right hand Joab took hold of Amasa’s beard as if to kiss him. Amasa was not on his guard against the sword in Joab’s [left] hand, and [Joab] drove it into his belly”
judaism.explanation: Joab greets his rival with a brotherly embrace while holding a sword in his other hand.
judaism.tie_back: A hand of greeting with a weapon hidden in the other is the Kural’s image made into history.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on a weapon concealed behind a gesture of affection.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Bilara Jataka, a jackal poses as a holy ascetic, standing on one leg and facing the sun in apparent worship. Rats come to pay him respect, and as they leave he seizes and eats the last of them each day, until the Bodhisatta, king of the rats, exposes him.
buddhism.explanation: A posture of worship is used as the cover for killing.
buddhism.tie_back: The jackal’s devotion is the worshipping hand that hides the weapon.
buddhism.source: Bilara Jataka (Jataka No. 128), trans. in E. B. Cowell (ed.), The Jataka
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; summarised from the well-known tale, not quoted.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “others were for letting it remain as an offering and propitiation for the gods. And this was how they settled it in the end, for the city was doomed when it took in that horse, within which were all the bravest of the Argives waiting to bring death and destruction on the Trojans.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Greeks’ apparent religious offering hides an army inside it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The wooden horse is a weapon hidden inside an act of worship, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on weapons concealed within worship; the ‘tears’ half has no parallel here.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The great advantages of simulation and dissimulation are three. First, to lay asleep opposition, and to surprise.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon notes coolly that a show which hides one’s true intent serves to disarm others and take them by surprise.
philosophy.tie_back: This is why the Kural warns of foes’ worship and tears: such shows are designed to lull us before the blow.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’
philosophy._accuracy_note: Explains the purpose behind feigned devotion, but is general analysis rather than a warning about foes’ tears.

kurals.tamil:
மிகச்செய்து தம்மெள்ளு வாரை நகச்செய்து
நட்பினுள் சாப்புல்லற் பாற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Migachcheythu thammellu vaarai nagachcheythu
natpinul saappullar̲ paat̲ru.
kurals.meaning: Those who make a great show of friendship while secretly despising you should be kept smiling on the surface, while you let that friendship die within yourself.
kurals.elementary: If a classmate is super-friendly to your face but laughs at you behind your back, you don’t have to start a fight. You can stay polite and friendly when you meet, but quietly stop trusting them and stop sharing your secrets.
kurals.university: Migachcheythu (மிகச்செய்து) is ‘making much of (friendship)’, and thammeḷḷuvaar (தம் எள்ளுவார்) are ‘those who scorn us’ within. The difficult phrase saappullaṟpaaṯru (சாப்புல்லற்பாற்று) is read by the commentators as ‘one should embrace (pullal) in such a way that it dies (saa)’: Varadarasanar says one should make them laugh in that friendship while acting so that the bond dies, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as answering pretence with pretence. Pope’s explanation, in the tradition of Parimelazhagar’s royal-political reading, presents this as the duty of kings toward such foes. Whether read as defensive policy or as cynicism, the couplet assumes a political setting where open rupture is costly; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If thou art angry, show thyself as if thou art not so, speaking even then with a smile on thy lips.”
hinduism.explanation: Kanika counsels Dhritarashtra to hide hostility behind a smiling manner in dealing with rivals.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s strategy of keeping the false friend smiling while one’s own inner friendship has ended.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 142, Kanika’s counsel (Ganguli translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the outward-smile tactic, but Kanika’s counsel is offensive and openly cynical, while the Kural is defensive.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples to combine shrewdness about hostile people with innocence of conduct.
christianity.tie_back: Both counsel staying outwardly peaceable while inwardly alert to those who mean harm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Partial match on wary gentleness; Jesus does not endorse feigned friendship.

islam.quote_or_event: “Let not believers take disbelievers as allies rather than believers. And whoever [of you] does that has nothing with Allah, except when taking precaution against them in prudence.”
islam.explanation: The verse forbids real alliance with hostile parties, while permitting outward caution in prudence.
islam.tie_back: The Kural similarly permits outward civility toward the scornful while withholding real friendship.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match on outward prudence without inner alliance; the legal scope of this exception is debated among commentators.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Absalom rebels against David, David’s loyal friend Hushai goes to Absalom, greets him warmly and appears to join him, but inwardly remains David’s man and defeats the dangerous advice of Ahithophel.
judaism.explanation: Outward friendship is offered to a hostile party while inner loyalty lies elsewhere.
judaism.tie_back: Hushai keeps Absalom pleased on the surface while the ‘friendship’ is dead within, as the Kural advises.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good structural match on feigned friendship toward a hostile party; summarised, not quoted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that hostility is ended only by non-hostility.
buddhism.tie_back: A contrast: the Kural answers pretence with pretence, while the Dhammapada asks one to drop hostility altogether.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Offered as a contrasting view; no close Buddhist parallel to strategic counter-pretence was found.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Back in Ithaca disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures the suitors’ mockery in his own house, keeping a calm face and even smiling grimly to himself, while he quietly prepares their destruction.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus answers scorn with outward composure while his inward attitude toward the suitors is settled.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Outward ease toward those who scorn you, inner withdrawal: the Kural’s strategy in epic form.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on hidden inner stance toward scorners; the suitors never pretended friendship, and the episode is summarised.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The best composition and temperature, is to have openness in fame and opinion; secrecy in habit; dissimulation in seasonable use; and a power to feign, if there be no remedy.”
philosophy.explanation: Bacon allows dissimulation and even feigning as a last resort, used only in season.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Bacon treats measured counter-pretence as legitimate prudence against those who deceive.
philosophy.source: Francis Bacon, Essays, ‘Of Simulation and Dissimulation’
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close match on permitted, limited dissimulation; Bacon speaks generally rather than about false friends.

kurals.tamil:
பகைநட்பாம் காலம் வருங்கால் முகநட்டு
அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Paganatpaam kaalam varungaal muganattu
aganatpu oreei vidal.
kurals.meaning: When the time comes that an enemy must be treated as a friend, be friendly in face, but keep friendship out of your heart, and let it go when you can.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes you have to work on a group project with someone who has been unkind to you. You can be polite and work together, but you don’t have to hand them your diary. Be friendly on the outside and careful on the inside.
kurals.university: Pagai-naṭpaam kaalam (பகை நட்பாம் காலம்) is ‘a time when enmity turns into friendship’, for instance an alliance forced by circumstances. The couplet resolves the chapter with the face/heart pair already used in Kural 824: muga-naṭṭu (முகநட்டு, befriending with the face) but aga-naṭpu oreei (அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ, removing friendship from the heart). Oreei (ஒரீஇ) is the alapeḍai-lengthened form of oree, ‘leaving’, and viḍal (விடல்) means ‘one should give it up’. Varadarasanar reads the final word as giving up even the outward friendship when the chance comes, Pappaiah as letting go of it in the mind, and Pope follows the first reading with ‘give up (even the former)’. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A weak person having made a compact with a stronger one when both are threatened by foes, should (when that common danger passes away) conduct himself heedfully and by considerations of policy. Having gained his object, the weaker of the two parties should not again repose confidence on the stronger.”
hinduism.explanation: The mouse Palita, who made a temporary alliance with the cat Lomasa to escape a hunter, refuses the cat’s invitations to continued friendship once the danger has passed.
hinduism.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural’s counsel: accept a necessary friendship with a foe, but never let it into the heart.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, Section 138, the cat and the mouse (Ganguli translation)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on outward alliance with a foe without inner trust.

christianity.quote_or_event: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.”
christianity.explanation: Paul urges believers to keep the peace with everyone so far as it depends on them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural too keeps outward peace with a former enemy, though it adds a caution Paul does not.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches outward peaceableness only; Paul does not counsel inner withdrawal, and his ethic leans toward reconciliation.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allah. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing. But if they intend to deceive you - then sufficient for you is Allah.”
islam.explanation: Believers are to accept a hostile party’s offer of peace, while recognising it may be a deception.
islam.tie_back: Accept the enemy’s turn to friendship outwardly, but keep your reliance elsewhere: the Kural’s balance.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on accepting peace with foes while staying alert; the Qur’an grounds security in God rather than inner withdrawal.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Jacob meets Esau after twenty years of enmity, they embrace and weep, and Esau offers to travel with him. Jacob graciously declines, sending Esau on ahead, and then settles in a different direction at Succoth.
judaism.explanation: Jacob accepts the reconciliation outwardly but does not put himself in his brother’s power.
judaism.tie_back: Friendly in face, guarded in heart: Jacob’s conduct matches the Kural’s advice.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match; summarised. Rabbinic readings differ on how sincere Esau’s embrace was.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who is friendly amidst the hostile, peaceful amidst the violent, and unattached amidst the attached — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada praises one who stays friendly and unattached in the midst of hostility.
buddhism.tie_back: Friendliness among the hostile without attachment loosely mirrors the Kural’s friendly face with an uncommitted heart.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Weak match: the Buddhist ideal is genuine goodwill, not strategic reserve.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After their single combat ends undecided at nightfall, Hector and Ajax exchange gifts, a sword and a belt, and part as men who fought in hatred but separated in friendship, yet they remain on opposite sides of the war.
greek_mythology.explanation: Enemies show each other the courtesies of friendship while remaining enemies.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A friendly face between foes without real alliance is the situation the Kural addresses.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Matches outward friendship between foes, but the exchange is honourable rather than guarded; summarised.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “they neither love warmly nor hate bitterly, but following the hint of Bias they love as though they will some day hate and hate as though they will some day love.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the guarded attitude of the experienced, following the sage Bias of Priene.
philosophy.tie_back: Loving ‘as though they will some day hate’ is the inner reserve the Kural advises toward a foe turned friend.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Rhetoric II.13 (trans. W. Rhys Roberts)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on inner reserve; Aristotle describes elderly character rather than giving advice.
